# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1-7 (Extended v79)

## Setting and Time
Multiple periods spanning French Revolution to 1826. **Current narrative point (Autumn Year 2, approximately late 1825 or late 1826)**: Valjean and Cosette in sanctuary at Convent of Petit-Picpus. Earlier markers: 1815 (Bishop's 75th birthday, Valjean's theft and flight; Waterloo/Hougomont June 17-18); 1817 (young Parisians' Saint-Cloud excursion); 1818 spring (Montfermeil, Thénardier family, Fantine's arrival); 1819-1821 (Madeleine's mayoral tenure); **1823 January (Fantine's arrest; Javert's revelation; TRIAL SEQUENCE in Arras; Valjean's self-revelation; acquittal of Champmathieu; arrest issued; RETURN TO M. SUR M. before six a.m.; Fantine's death; Valjean arrested beside death-bed; VALJEAN ESCAPES same evening)**; December 1823 (Montfermeil rescue of Cosette, 1,500-franc payment to Thénardier); **December 26, 1823 (Valjean and Cosette returned to Paris via Barrier Monceaux)**; 1824 spring onward (decrepit building lodging; winter passed; spring advanced); **Summer Year 2**: Achieved sanctuary inside walled garden compound, le Petit-Picpus district.

## Primary Locations
M. sur M.; Montfermeil (between Livry and Chelles); English harbor towns (Dunstead/Kelford/Ravenmere/Staveford); Arras; Waterloo; Toulon; Paris districts including Mouffetard quarter (Rue Censier, Rue Copeau, Rue du Battoir-Saint-Victor, Rue du Puits l'Ermite, Rue de Pontoise; commissary office No. 14; Saint-Étienne-du-Mont church); **Gorbeau House (Rue de la Cosette area, Mouffetard)**: Decrepit lodging, old woman portress, Javert's surveillance station. **Cul-de-Sac de la Planchette**: Pewter Platter tavern departure point. **Mouffetard escape**: Street lantern rope cut; Javert misled toward Cul-de-Sac Genrot (blind alley with low walls, gardens, waste stretches). **LE PETIT-PICPUS DISTRICT**: Between Faubourg Saint-Antoine and la Râpée; market-gardens, timber-yards, unpaved roads, monkish solitude. **Rue Petit-Picpus and Rue Droit-Mur**: Mean houses and severe building. **Number 62 Rue Petit-Picpus (CONVENT CARRIAGE GATE)**: Ajar gate, courtyard surrounded by vine-hung walls, porter visible, tall trees above wall. **Wall (approximately 18 feet)**: Extends from niche to house 49 Rue Polonceau; shorter fragment along Rue Droit-Mur. **CONVENT OF THE BERNARDINES OF THE PERPETUAL ADORATION**: Gloomy building, one heavily shuttered window with sheet zinc, ancient cistern pipes, linden-tree with ivy, interior façades tragic with grated windows, upper story scuttles resembling prison cells. **INTERIOR GARDEN**: Vast oblong area; alley of large poplars; forest trees in corners; unshaded central space with solitary gnarled tree, fruit-trees, vegetable beds, melon patch with glass frames, old well, stone benches, gloomy bordered alleys, grass and green mould; roof descends from wooden barricade top to gentle slope. **PARLOR (Convent Communication Chamber)**: Theatre-box-like narrow space, two old chairs, frayed straw matting, sparse light from glass door; front bears black wooden tablet; monstrous lattice of interlaced iron bars (squares less than 1.5 inches diagonal) riveted by clenched-fist fastenings; behind lattice: barrier of black shutters reinforced with gingerbread-yellow wooden beams divided into slats, always closed; behind shutters: nun's voice screened by iron grating and plate with thousand holes; when rare conditions permit, slat opens revealing nun's mouth and chin only, rest covered with black veil, black guimpe, black shroud; speaks without looking or smiling; window on world-side only; quadrangular hole one foot square with interlacing iron bars; reinforced by sheet of tin with thousand microscopic holes; aperture bottom like letter-box orifice; tape attached to bell-wire at right.

## Convent of the Bernardines of the Perpetual Adoration (Comprehensive Details)
**Order Lineage**: Bernardines-Benedictines of Martin Verga obedience; Benedictine order founded 529 by Saint-Benoît (aged seventeen) chasing devil from Apollo temple in Subiaco desert; spawned nine orders including Cîteaux (1098), Carthusians, Cluny, Saint-Maur, Vallombrosa, Granmont, Célestins, Camaldules, Humiliés, Olivateurs, Silvestrins. **Dress**: Black clothing with white guimpe mounting to chin per Saint-Benoît's command; serge robe with large sleeves; large woollen veil; band descending over brow to eyes (white); novices wear all-white; professed nuns wear rosary at side. **Austerity**: Fast all year; abstain from meat; additional fasting in Lent and peculiar days; rise one to three a.m. for breviary and matins; sleep year-round on straw between serge sheets; never light fires; never bathe; scourge every Friday; strict silence except brief recreation; wear drugget chemises September 14 (Exaltation of Holy Cross) to Easter—originally year-round but summer fevers and spasms caused modification; resumed chemise causes three-to-four-day fever even with modification. **Vows**: Obedience, poverty, chastity, perseverance in seclusion; rule greatly aggravates vows. **Operational Rules**: Never see officiating priest (hidden behind nine-foot serge curtain); drop veils during sermons; speak low; walk with eyes down and heads bowed; only diocesan archbishop permitted entry; absolute passive submission to prioress (canonical subjection—at Christ's voice, at gesture, at first sign, immediately with cheerfulness, perseverance, blind obedience, like file in workman's hand); cannot read or write without express permission. **Reparation Practice**: Each nun in turn performs twelve-hour continuous reparation prayer (either 4 p.m. to 4 a.m. or 4 a.m. to 4 p.m.) on knees on stone before Holy Sacrament, hands clasped, rope around neck; when fatigue unbearable, prostrates flat against earth, arms outstretched as cross; prays for all guilty in universe. **Possessions Rule**: Never say "my"; call everything "our" (our veil, our chaplet, our chemise); if grow attached to petty object (book of hours, relic, blessed medal), must surrender it immediately per Saint Thérèse's teaching. **Lodging**: Never shut themselves up; cannot have chamber of own; cells open; when meeting, one says "Blessed and adored be the most Holy Sacrament of the altar!" other responds "Forever!"; same ceremony when tapping at door; becomes mechanical by habit, sometimes "Forever!" spoken before full sentence completed. **Hourly Bells**: At each hour three supplementary church bell strokes; prioress, vocal mothers, professed nuns, lay-sisters, novices, postulants interrupt all activity and say in unison formula like "At five o'clock and at all hours praised and adored be the most Holy Sacrament of the altar!" **Variations**: Other communities like The Infant Jesus say "At this hour and at every hour may the love of Jesus kindle my heart!"; Bernardines-Benedictines of Martin Verga, cloistered fifty years ago at Petit-Picpus, chant offices to solemn psalmody, pure Gregorian chant, full voice throughout; pause at asterisk in missal, say low "Jesus-Marie-Joseph"; for office of dead adopt tone so low women's voices can barely descend to such depth—effect striking and tragic. **Burial Issue**: Vault beneath grand altar for community burials; Government forbids coffin burial in vault, so nuns leave convent when die—causes consternation as infraction of rules. **Friday Observances**: High mass, vespers, all offices as on Sunday; scrupulously observe little festivals unknown to world, which Church of France was prodigal with in olden days and still is in Spain and Italy; stations in chapel interminable; prayers of postulants "frightful," novices "still worse," professed nuns "still worse." **Visitor Communication**: Prioress alone holds communication with strangers; others see only immediate family, very rarely; if outsider presents self to see nun, regular negotiations required; if woman, authorization sometimes granted—nun comes, they talk through shutters opened only for mother or sister; permission always refused to men. **Profession Ceremony**: Novice dressed in handsomest attire, crowned with white roses, hair brushed until shining and curled; prostrates herself; great black veil thrown over her; office for dead sung; nuns separate into two files; one file passes close saying in plaintive accents "Our sister is dead"; other file responds in voice of ecstasy "Our sister is alive in Jesus Christ!" **Pupils**: Conform to all practices except austerities; some former pupils never break habit of saying "forever!" when door knocked—saw relatives only in parlor, mothers not permitted to embrace them; example: young girl received mother's visit with three-year-old sister; wept to embrace sister but permission impossible; begged child be permitted to pass little hand through bars to kiss—almost indignantly refused. **Children's Observations**: Child of five exclaimed "Mother! one of the big girls has just told me that I have only nine years and ten months longer to remain here. What happiness!" **Refectory Locations**: Four corners designated Cricket, etc.; Cricket corner near kitchen, highly esteemed, less cold than elsewhere; names passed from refectory to boarding-school to distinguish four nations per old College Mazarin system; every pupil belonged to one nation according to refectory seating. **Archbishop's Visit Observation**: During pastoral visit, Monseigneur Archbishop saw pretty little rosy girl with beautiful golden hair enter class-room.

## Jean Valjean's Current Sanctuary Status
**ESCAPE FROM M. SUR M.** (January 1823 evening): Successfully fled jail after Javert's arrest beside Fantine's death-bed; climbed 18-foot wall using muscular force; placed Cosette on back; descended safely to interior garden via roof. **REFUGE DISCOVERY AND FAUCHELEVENT**: Encountered elderly crippled gardener Fauchelevent, admitted to convent approximately two years previously (1821) on Mayor Madeleine's recommendation after falling from cart; explained bell-sound as kneecap device during melon-bed work. **PSYCHOLOGICAL STATE**: So long as Cosette near, needs nothing except her, fears nothing except her; experiencing continual tremor; distrust of day and night equally. **COSETTE**: Now sleeping in Fauchelevent's bed; rosy; completely dependent on Valjean. **CURRENT LOCATION** (Autumn Year 2): Still secured in convent sanctuary wearing cravat and coat; hat recovered. **ALTERED APPEARANCE**: Sadness, uneasiness, anxiety, depression from nighttime flight and regulating pace to child's pace have altered his walk and impressed senility on bearing such that police themselves (Javert) made mistake in doubting his identity.

## Fauchelevent (Elderly Gardener—Established Ally)
**Identity**: Old crippled gardener; admitted to convent approximately two years previously on Valjean's (Mayor Madeleine's) recommendation after cart accident. **Character**: Grateful, talkative, excitable; reproaches Valjean for not recognizing him, calls him "Father Madeleine," accuses ingratitude despite saved life; speaks freely about work. **Current Occupation**: Spreading straw mats over melon beds in garden; wears bell and kneecap device. **Hospitality**: Provided Cosette safe bed; offered cheese, black bread, wine; warming themselves at table in his quarters. **Status**: Valjean's only known ally and protector in Paris; sole person aware of Valjean and Cosette's presence.

## Javert's Pursuit and Strategic Hesitation
**REASSIGNMENT TO PARIS** (January 1823): When Valjean escaped M. sur M. jail, police supposed Paris destination; Javert summoned; zeal and intelligence remarked by M. Chabouillet, secretary of Prefecture under Comte Anglès; Javert (already Chabouillet's patron) attached to Paris police force circa 1823. **NEWSPAPER REPORT** (December 1823): Newspaper announced Valjean's death in formal terms; Javert read, remarked "That's a good entry," threw paper aside, thought no more. **REACTIVATION**: Police report from Seine-et-Oise prefecture concerning child abduction in Montfermeil; Javert's memory revived—recalled Fantine's name, remembered Valjean asked three-day respite to fetch her child, remembered Valjean arrested in Paris stepping into Montfermeil-bound coach; suspected Valjean had made previous excursion seeking Fantine's daughter; understood: Fantine's daughter in Montfermeil, Valjean seeking her, child stolen by stranger—could stranger be Valjean? But Valjean was dead. **JAVERT'S SECRET INVESTIGATION**: Without telling anyone, took coach from Pewter Platter tavern (Cul-de-Sac de la Planchette) to Montfermeil; followed mysterious lodger to Gorbeau house; got old woman portress talking—she confirmed coat-lined-with-millions episode and thousand-franc bill; hired room same evening, installed himself; listened at mysterious lodger's door hoping to catch voice; Valjean saw candle through key-hole, foiled spy by silence. **REASONS FOR SECRECY** (Three Motives): (1) Slightest indiscretion might alert Valjean; (2) To recapture ex-convict reputed dead, classified as most dangerous malefactor, was magnificent success—old Parisian police would not leave to newcomer Javert, feared being deprived; (3) Javert, being artist, had taste for unforeseen—hated well-heralded successes talked in advance with bloom brushed off; preferred elaborating masterpieces in dark, unveiling suddenly at last. **PURSUIT ESCALATION**: Following day Valjean noticed five-franc piece falling; old woman heard rattling coin, suspected lodger intending to leave, warned Javert; at night when Valjean came out, Javert waited behind trees with two men. **ESCAPE FROM MOUFFETARD**: Valjean cut street lantern rope; Javert found disorder in lantern—precious sign which led him astray, turning researches toward Cul-de-Sac Genrot; explored gardens and waste stretches as hunting for needle; had he penetrated further, probably would have caught Valjean and been lost. **JAVERT'S HESITATION AND PSYCHOLOGICAL TORMENT**: Javert followed Valjean from tree to tree, corner to corner, had not lost sight single instant; why had not arrested Valjean? Because still in doubt. **STRATEGIC CALCULATION**: Considered abrupt demand for papers risky—if man was not Valjean, and was honest old fellow living on income, probably some merry blade deeply and cunningly implicated in Parisian misdeeds, chief of dangerous band giving alms to conceal talents; had trusty fellows, accomplices' retreat emergencies; all street turns indicated not simple honest man; to arrest hastily would be "to kill the hen that laid the golden eggs." Where inconvenience in waiting? Javert very sure man would not escape. **PSYCHOLOGICAL TORMENT**: Began the game—experienced ecstatic and infernal moment; allowed man to go ahead, knowing had him safe, but desiring postponing moment of arrest as long as possible, happy thinking he was taken yet seeing him free, gloating with gaze with voluptuousness of spider allowing fly to flutter, of cat letting mouse run; claws and talons possess monstrous sensuality; obscure movements of creature imprisoned in pincers; what delight this strangling is! **MOMENT OF LOSS**: Even at moment when saw Valjean had escaped, Javert did not lose head; sure convict could not be far off, established sentinels, organized traps and ambuscades, beat quarter all that night. **IMPEDIMENT TO ARREST**: Free press embarrassed police; several arbitrary arrests denounced by newspapers echoed as far as Chambers, rendered Prefecture timid; interference with individual liberty grave matter; police agents afraid of mistakes; prefect laid blame; mistake meant dismissal. Paragraph of grandfather with white hair arrested as escaped convict would have caused effect in Paris—reproduced by twenty newspapers.

## English Harbor Towns Communities (Secondary Setting)
Named residents: Matho Stenson, Ismira Stenson, Pelde Stenson, Harine Lindmere, Davus Stenworth, Havus Stenworth, Yera, Orrald the Younger, Orrald Stenson, Fewyn Stenworth. **Movements**: Havus Stenworth rode out of Torton; by next market day living in Gulhaven. Fewyn Stenworth followed him within the month. **Activities and Observations**: Reading almanacs aloud with mispronounced saints; sorting letters by candlelight (Pelde); discussing weather, harvest, lame horse, salt prices (Pelde and Harine); Orrald complained of aching back; rumor of Dunstead granary fire set on purpose; frost silvered hedges overnight; wind from water with salt and tar smell; bees humming in lavender; crooked sun chalked on forge wall (cricket corner near kitchen, highly esteemed); baker's boy late, line at oven long; cart loaded with turnips creaked past well; rain threatening since morning but held off; children chased hoop down lane shrieking; light went early; smoke from chimneys lay flat over fields; Pelde laughed at story nobody else found funny; Davus laughed at story nobody else found funny; Pelde hummed tune from childhood while scrubbing step.
